title: Ethics, Integrity & Professional Judgment
summary: Learn how ethics, integrity, policy, responsibility, and professional judgment work together when workplace decisions are not always simple.
objectives: Explain ethics and integrity in a workplace context.
Distinguish what is technically possible from what is authorized or appropriate.
Identify when a situation requires clarification, escalation, or human judgment.

vocab.def: Principles used to evaluate what is responsible, fair, honest, and appropriate.
Acting consistently with honest and responsible standards, including when no one is watching.
Using evidence, policy, role boundaries, consequences, and responsible reasoning to decide what action is appropriate.
An established organizational rule, requirement, or standard that guides decisions and behavior.

sections.heading: Ethics begins where choices affect other people
sections.body: Workplace decisions can affect coworkers, customers, communities, information, safety, money, trust, and reputation. Ethical work considers more than whether an action is easy or technically possible.

sections.heading: Integrity connects words and actions
sections.body: Integrity includes being truthful about what you know, what you completed, what went wrong, and what still requires review. It also means not claiming results that have not been established.

sections.heading: Policy and ethics often work together
sections.body: Policies help define expected behavior, permissions, approvals, and boundaries. When a rule is unclear, the responsible response may be to ask rather than guess.

sections.heading: Professional judgment includes knowing when to stop
sections.body: A worker may need to pause when information is incomplete, authority is unclear, consequences are significant, or a decision belongs to a more qualified or authorized person.

practice.prompt: You are able to change a record in a system, but the change normally requires manager approval. Does technical access alone make the change appropriate?
practice.answer: No. Technical capability does not replace the required authorization or approval process.

practice.prompt: You are asked whether a project is complete, but one important review is still pending. What is the most ethical response?
practice.answer: State the actual status accurately and explain that the required review is still pending.

quiz.question: Which action best demonstrates workplace integrity?
options: Report the actual status accurately even when the result is incomplete
Claim success before required review is finished
Hide mistakes if no one notices them
Treat technical access as permission to take any action
quiz.answer: Report the actual status accurately even when the result is incomplete

lab.objective: Review simulated workplace decisions involving incomplete information, authorization, policy, and reporting, then identify the most responsible next step.

reflectionPrompt: Why can telling the truth about an incomplete result sometimes require more integrity than reporting success?
